read_from: The route text as served, in the extract this reissue counts (the serving lane's merge of 7 November 2026 AD: the route store's rows of this source followed by the span store's records of it; a span record is one JSON per line with key, route, def, m, year and cut, and the span store's own fields, which are not marks). The route store's rows: field 1 (the route text) of each row of reader/data/route-store of the main branch at commit 1d2470eb356b, store_version 3d8c4ef86c01 (its index.json; the store served on 7 November 2026 AD, 652,885 routes in all), for "Open Scriptures Hebrew Lexical Index" (M33): 138 routes (axis: routes), byte for byte the 138 routes of the store of 31 October (commit 306f3b285898, store_version 87b13b1169b4) that the ledger of v139 read. The span store's records: the 198 records of this source in the span store as served (schema span-store-served-v1, from span-store-v2.1, dictionary store cc890b8a7992, ledgers applied on 2026-11-07; 1,698 records in all, axis: records), each a name or a phrase of two or more Hebrew words read as one, with its own route text, which the classifier reads like any route. Together 336 routes (axis: routes), 326 letters keys (axis: keys). The definition field of the same row equals the route text on 336 of the routes. The source audit (builder/02-audit.mjs of v139, evidence about the source and no part of any test) covers the route store's rows: the source is the Open Scriptures HebrewLexicon's LexicalIndex.xml, and each of those 138 routes equals, exactly, the one definition element of an entry filed under the same letters, as the dictionary store's records of M33 show; all 339 records there hold one definition element each. So such a route comes from one field, and no test here stands on a guess about a field. The span store's records were not audited against the source's file here; their texts are of the same kinds as the route store's (a name, with or without a pointing word, a margin note or a bracket), and the span store's own fields were not read for any test. The source's own key is on file: its documentation at commit 21c9add13bc7 (<tabernacle>/corpus-lane-builds/moses-works-own-stamp-v1/strand-1-the-old-books/fetch/M5-openscriptures-HebrewLexicon-21c9add.pdf.txt, the section Lexical Index). It says that the definition element holds a simple definition, in general the first BDB definition, and for a proper name the first Strong usage, with problematic cases decided on their own merit. Of the signs in these routes it speaks of none: its 341 lines hold no line that names the margin, the word Compare, the article, a hyphen, a full stop or a plural ending; its 1 line with the word See sends the reader to a list of language codes, and its 1 line that names parentheses speaks of how BDB numbers its senses (source-audit/key-search.json of v139). A second key stands on file for one sign: the section SIGNS EMPLOYED of Strong's own plan (<tabernacle>/corpus-lane-builds/moses-works-own-stamp-v1/strand-1-the-old-books/fetch/M14-strongs-scan-first12pages.txt, the text of a scan). It says that round brackets in the renderings from the King James Version denote a word or syllable sometimes given with the principal word to which it is annexed. It reaches the 2 rows with an ending in round brackets, because the source files each as a name and takes a name's text from the first Strong usage, and by entry number each Strong's list opens with the row's exact text. That section names no hyphen. So the two round-bracket shapes of those rows name the plan and do not begin "unverified:", the hyphen's meaning keeps it and says the plan backs its reading only, and the meaning of 18 of the 20 shapes begins "unverified:".

definitions.terms: In every test a character is one Unicode code point (every route holds only characters of 16 bits, so a code point is one index of the JavaScript string). No test asks for a letter, a digit or whitespace, or for uppercase or lowercase as a class. A space is the character U+0020 and no other. Nothing is trimmed: the text is the whole route text as it stands, which is the field route of a line of the by-source JSONL, what the checker gives the classifier, and never the field def. The text after the mark is the template's c.after. What the bracket holds is the template's c.group: the text between this bracket and its partner, as it stands. What the bracket around the mark holds is the template's c.inner: the text inside the innermost bracket the mark sits in, as it stands. Exactly means equal character for character. A string stands between « and », which are not part of it; a full stop after » belongs to the sentence. Every string and every list minds case and is matched exact to the character. No test uses the words begins with or contains.
definitions.first_match: For each mark the shapes are tried in the order they stand in this file; the first whose test holds names the occurrence, and no later shape is tried for it. A shape's container field is not part of its test: no test here looks at the container, and the checker compares the field afterwards. An occurrence that no shape of its mark takes makes the classifier throw, and none does: no shape here takes an occurrence without a test.
definitions.unbalanced: The ask's helper of rule 3, unchanged. Read the text from its first character to its last with an empty stack. At an opener, one of «(», «[», «<», «{», put it on the stack. At a closer, one of «)», «]», «>», «}»: if the stack holds something and its top is this closer's own opener, take the top off; otherwise stop, the text does not balance. If the stack still holds something after the last character, the text does not balance. Otherwise it balances.
definitions.before_a_pointing_word: Two steps, in order. One: the character directly after the mark is a space; where the mark ends the text no character stands there and the step fails. Two: the text after that space, to the end of the text, is exactly one of the strings in pointing_words.

homonyms.reason: The route text carries no entry number. The source's own file gives each entry an id and, in its cross-reference element, a Strong's, BDB or TWOT number, and the store dropped them (the dictionary store's record keeps them). Each entry holds one definition, so by the audit each of the 4 keys of the route store's rows with more than one text (axis: keys) has a different entry behind each text (example key שמיר, whose 2 texts come from 2 entries), though the route text cannot tell two entries from two spellings of one name. The span store's records add 2 such keys, two spellings of one name under one key (חצר עינון: Hazar-enon and Hazar-enan), not audited against the source here, and 0 keys whose two texts stand one in the route store and one in the span store; together 6 keys (axis: keys). 3 routes of the route store's rows stand for two or more entries that share letters and text, which the route text cannot show at all.

branches.question: Some rows give a word or a name and then words that lead nowhere: Kadesh. Compare. That last word points at another entry without naming it, and in another row a bracket breaks off inside a word. Those words are no reading. Today the page prints each such row as one reading, as written, and from the day this ledger is wired it still does, unless you choose otherwise. A cut would print those words as a reading of their own, so no answer here cuts. Should the page print only what stands before them? A declaration cannot leave words out, so that answer needs one step of the page's own.
